description:
Barberstown Castle stands near Straffan in County Kildare, and its documented history stretches back further than almost any other property in this collection: the castle was built in 1288 by Nicholas Barby, whose name gives the castle its own — 'Barberstown' derives directly from 'Barby's town.' That construction date places Barberstown's origins in the same broad period as many of the great Norman castles of medieval Ireland, and more than 730 years of continuous history since then make it one of the oldest inhabited castles in the entire country, a claim relatively few properties anywhere can genuinely support with this depth of documented age.

The castle's medieval history was shaped directly by its position within 'the Pale,' the fortified and defended territory surrounding Dublin that marked the practical limit of secure English control in medieval Ireland. Barberstown formed part of this defensive network, and its position exposed it to repeated attack over roughly two centuries from Gaelic clans based beyond the Pale's boundary, including the Uí Faoláin among others. This sustained military pressure over generations reflects the genuinely contested nature of the frontier zone Barberstown occupied throughout much of the medieval period, a border castle in the fullest sense rather than a purely ceremonial or residential structure.

Barberstown's more recent history includes one of the more unexpected celebrity connections found anywhere in this collection: the castle was owned by the musician Eric Clapton between 1979 and 1987. During his ownership, Clapton reportedly held informal jam sessions with fellow rock musicians within the castle's own named spaces — the 'Green Room' and the 'Castle Keep' — turning a medieval Irish fortification into an impromptu venue for some of the era's most celebrated rock musicians to play together informally, away from the pressures of official studio or concert settings. This episode gives Barberstown a genuinely distinctive place in popular music history alongside its much longer medieval military record.

The castle has operated as a country house hotel since 1971, considerably predating Clapton's period of ownership and continuing well beyond it into the property's current identity. Today Barberstown offers 55 rooms, a scale that positions it comfortably among Ireland's mid-sized luxury castle hotels, set within 20 acres of grounds that give guests space to explore beyond the historic building itself. The property holds membership in both Ireland's Blue Book, a long-established association of the country's finest country house hotels and restaurants, and Historic Hotels of Europe, a wider continental network recognising genuinely historic properties — memberships that reflect Barberstown's recognised standing within Ireland's heritage hospitality sector specifically, beyond its own individually striking history.

County Kildare itself is closely associated with Ireland's horse-racing and bloodstock industry, home to the Irish National Stud and the Curragh racecourse, giving the wider region a distinctive character built around equestrian tradition alongside its historic estates and castles. Barberstown's location within this landscape places it naturally within reach of Kildare's racing and stud farm attractions, adding a further dimension of interest for visitors with an interest in horses and racing alongside the castle's own layered history.

For visitors seeking one of Ireland's most historically documented castle stays, combined with a genuinely unexpected chapter of rock music history, Barberstown Castle offers a compelling combination: more than seven centuries of continuous habitation, real medieval border-warfare history, and a decade under the ownership of one of rock music's most celebrated guitarists, all within a single, still-operating hotel property in the Kildare countryside.

The castle's later Elizabethan and Victorian-era additions layer further architectural periods onto the original 13th-century tower, giving Barberstown a genuinely composite building history spanning several distinct eras of Irish architecture rather than a single unified style. Guest rooms today are distributed across these different wings and periods of construction, meaning a stay at Barberstown can involve rooms of noticeably different character depending on which part of the building's long architectural evolution a particular guest room occupies — a detail that adds a further layer of tangible historical texture to the experience of staying within a building this genuinely old.
history: Barberstown Castle was built in 1288 by Nicholas Barby, from whom it takes its name, and has more than 730 years of continuous history, making it one of the oldest inhabited castles in Ireland. It formed part of the fortifications of the Pale, the defended territory around Dublin, and was repeatedly attacked over two centuries by the Uí Faoláin and other Gaelic clans. The castle was owned by musician Eric Clapton from 1979 to 1987, who held informal jam sessions with fellow rock stars in its Green Room and Castle Keep. Barberstown has operated as a country house hotel since 1971, with 55 rooms, and is a member of Ireland's Blue Book and Historic Hotels of Europe.

faqs.question: Is it true that Eric Clapton owned Barberstown Castle?
faqs.answer: Yes. The musician Eric Clapton owned Barberstown Castle from 1979 to 1987, and reportedly held informal jam sessions with fellow rock musicians in the castle's named 'Green Room' and 'Castle Keep' spaces during his ownership.

faqs.answer: Barberstown Castle was built in 1288 by Nicholas Barby, from whom it takes its name, giving it more than 730 years of continuous history and making it one of the oldest inhabited castles in Ireland.

faqs.question: What was Barberstown Castle's role in medieval Ireland?
faqs.answer: Barberstown formed part of the fortifications of the Pale, the defended territory surrounding Dublin that marked the limit of secure English control in medieval Ireland. It was repeatedly attacked over roughly two centuries by the Uí Faoláin and other Gaelic clans based beyond the Pale's boundary.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** Straffan, Co. Kildare, 40 minutes from Dublin.

**Rooms & rates:** All 55 rooms and suites are in the adjacent Elizabethan and Georgian manor-house wings — not in the 13th-century castle tower itself, which today houses the Medieval Banqueting Hall (1562) used for private events and dinners rather than guest bedrooms.

**On-site:** Restaurant, gardens, the historic Green Room and Castle Keep bar area associated with Eric Clapton's ownership (1979-87).

**Good to know:** If 'sleeping in the actual medieval tower' is the goal, this isn't it — the appeal here is staying on genuinely 700+ year-old grounds and dining in the historic hall, not sleeping inside it.

**Combine with:** Castletown House (15 minutes) for a Kildare country-house circuit.
